cards.target: Jisses, det var verkligen oväntat men väldigt positivt!
cards.english: Gosh, it was really unexpected but very positive!

cards.target: Hon planterade nya rosor i trädgården förra våren.
cards.english: She planted new roses in the garden last spring.

cards.target: Vi provade lokala delikatesser på marknaden i lördags.
cards.english: We tried local delicacies at the market last Saturday.

cards.target: De byggde ett nytt hus vid kusten förra sommaren.
cards.english: They built a new house by the coast last summer.

cards.target: Vi spelade kort i flera timmar och skrattade mycket.
cards.english: We played cards for several hours and laughed a lot.

cards.target: Hon sydde en ny klänning till festen förra helgen.
cards.english: She sewed a new dress for the party last weekend.

cards.target: Barnen frågade oss varför vi inte kunde stanna längre.
cards.english: The children asked us why we could not stay longer.

cards.target: Jag måste ringa tandläkaren och boka en tid snart.
cards.english: I must call the dentist and book an appointment soon.

cards.target: Barnen sprang runt i trädgården tills det blev mörkt.
cards.english: The children ran around in the garden until it got dark.

existing_tips: Swedish loves compound nouns – long words made of smaller ones. `Tandborste` = tooth + brush. Break
Ordinal dates use -e or -te endings: femtonde = fifteenth. Swedish dates go day-month.
"Får" = may/allowed to. "Får inte" = must not / not allowed to.
"Igår" first → "regnade" second → "det" third. This is V2 inversion.
"Kan du" + infinitive is the standard polite request format.
"Ska ha" + supine = reportedly/supposedly. Distances from the claim.
Exclamatory word order: "Vad" + adjective + subject + verb.
"Måste" has no infinitive form – it's always "måste" in all tenses.
"Er" is both 'you' (object, plural) and 'your.' Context determines the meaning.
Indirect question as subject: "Var hon bor" = where she lives.
After att, när, om, eftersom: inte (not) goes before the verb. Jag vet att han inte kommer (I know t
Reported questions use "om" (if/whether) for yes/no questions.
In subordinate clauses after "var/att/om": subject + inte + verb.
"Kan" means both 'can' and 'know how to.' No 'att' before the infinitive after modals.
Reported questions with wh-words keep the question word: var, när, hur, etc.
